title: "Can I see a proper doctor?"
topic: Responding to criticism, feedback and your own underperformance
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in paediatrics. You have just examined Noah, 3, who has a fever and a rash. You hesitated while explaining your findings to his mother.

She says, "You don't seem sure. Can I see a proper doctor?"
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Explain that you are a fully qualified doctor.
options.detailed: This may be true, but it doesn't address her concern.

options.text: Tell her the registrar is too busy.
options.detailed: This leaves her worried and doesn't help Noah.

options.text: Acknowledge her concern calmly, without becoming defensive.
options.brief: Her worry is about Noah, not you.
options.detailed: She is worried about her son. A calm response helps keep her trust.

options.text: Offer to ask your registrar to review Noah.
options.brief: Senior input may reassure her and check your assessment.
options.detailed: A fever and rash in a young child can be serious, and a senior review is reasonable. It also respects her request.

options.text: Ask her to be more respectful.
options.detailed: Her comment may hurt, but she's anxious about her child.

options.text: Insist on completing your assessment before anyone else sees him.
options.brief: Prioritises your role over her concern.
options.detailed: Completing your assessment is fine, but refusing senior input isn't.

options.text: Leave, and ask the nurse to find another doctor.
options.detailed: This leaves the family without a clear plan.

options.text: Reflect afterwards on how you explained your findings.
options.detailed: Thinking about why you hesitated may help you communicate more clearly in future.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond professionally when a parent questions your competence.
explanation.keyDetails: Noah has a fever and rash. You hesitated. His mother is worried.
explanation.reasoning: [C] stays calm, [D] offers senior input, and [H] reflects. The distractors are defensive ([A], [E], [F]), dismissive ([B]), or avoidant ([G]).
explanation.competing: [A] is the tempting option, but it doesn't address her worry.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 1, reflecting on your practice; Domain 2, responding to patients' concerns.
